rites.name: Braston
rites.text: Braston is the concept of the unbroken hum that carried through Halardore during the Singing, before its first roots had settled into soil. It is less a force than a pattern of tension that lets the forming world hold together long enough to take shape.

rites.name: Oriannimora
rites.text: Oriannimora is the concept of a fixed sounding within Halardore, the tone by which the first roots of the world were held together before they took shape. It is remembered as the note that every landfall in the Age of Sundering struck against, cracking the old bonds that had once kept shores joined.

rites.name: Tensaeno
rites.text: Tensaeno is a concept of the Halardore Courts, a notion of trial and judgment as the councils weighed each claim before the doors between worlds were raised. In the Holy Age of flame and temples, it was taught as the discipline by which orders tested their own vows against the fire. It was never a single being, only a measure the orders carried into every hall.

rites.name: Lyirla
rites.text: Lyirla is a concept in the Halardore cosmos, born in the Courts during the era of divine trials and the building of the doors between worlds. Within the Holy Age of flame, temples and orders, it is understood as a principle of hearth-fire that binds the orders to their vows. It remains a grounded idea, expressed through rites rather than cataclysm.

rites.name: Gagok
rites.text: Gagok is a concept of Halardore's Seeding, the stillness in which makers pressed the Weave into the soil and the quiet powers lay dormant. It names the reason groves took root and sovereigns first learned to hold land in common. It is not a being, but the frame the early kingdoms grew within.

rites.name: Kaizhun
rites.text: Kaizhun is a concept of Halardore's Holy Age, born in the years after the Fall and the Sundering, when the Pact was sworn among the orders that rose from the broken worlds. It names the discipline of holding a single flame steady through the long nights of the Shards, a practice that temples across the age taught as both prayer and craft.

rites.name: Tenlavalira
rites.text: Tenlavalira is a concept in Halardore, an idea that the Fall, the Sundering and the Shards all turned on: the belief that a broken world could be bound again by a sworn word. During the Holy Age, its name was carved above the gates of flame-lit temples and taught by the orders as the first clause of the Pact.

rites.name: Siathith
rites.text: Siathith is a concept in Halardore's Walled Age, a notion of a lattice of holding walls that the orders raised to keep their groves and first crossings safe. It is remembered in the churches as the principle by which early kingdoms measured what a wall could hold back.

rites.name: Ilovaneno
rites.text: Ilovaneno is a concept from the Walled Age of Halardore, a principle of holding that the great orders taught to bind their walls against the sea. Its adherents believed a wall was only as strong as the oath that raised it, and the idea spread through churches and first crossings during the Age of Sundering.

rites.name: Tastium
rites.text: Tastium is a concept in the Halardore setting, a notion of how flavor and sensation can be bent into a lasting pattern during the Three Futures. It is shelved in the Library as one of the branching outcomes that the Record keeps for later reading.

rites.name: Shasteizeth
rites.text: Shasteizeth is a concept within Halardore, a grounded realm where the Three Futures are kept as shelved branches of the Library. During the Holy Age of flame, temples and orders, it names the principle that a single chosen outcome can be read off from many possible endings. It is held as an idea rather than a physical presence, and its influence is felt in the rituals and disciplines of the period.

rites.name: Ilovaneno
rites.text: Ilovaneno is a concept held in the Library of Halardore, a shelved idea of how the Three Futures might branch when the ending splits. It takes shape during the Age of Sundering, when landfall broke old bonds between settlements and their keepers.
